newsitem.title: UK: Car bomb against Sinn Fein defused in N. Ireland. [CORRECTED 22:56 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Car bomb against Sinn Fein defused in N. Ireland. [CORRECTED 22:56 GMT]

text.p: Pro-British Loyalists planted a bomb outside the offices of their pro-Irish rivals, Sinn Fein, on Sunday as Irish republicans marked the 1916 Dublin rising against British rule.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, said the car bomb was "designed to murder" and openly blamed Loyalist groups, who are supposed to be observing an October 1994 ceasefire.
Police carried out controlled explosions on the car, which was left close to the office of Sinn Fein, the IRA guerrillas' political arm, in the New Lodge area of Belfast.
Mayhew also condemned the Irish Republican Army for an overnight sniper attack at Forkhill, county Armagh, in which a policeman was seriously injured.
He said the message from the rival guerrilla groups was "that the organisations concerned still rely upon death and destruction to secure what they want in this democracy."

Sinn Fein is barred from Belfast peace talks after the IRA ended a 17-month truce in February 1996 (corrects from 1994) but Loyalist groups are taking part because their umbrella organisation maintains that its own truce is intact, despite attacks it blames on mavericks.
Sources close to the Loyalist groups say near-daily IRA violence has put their truce under immense strain and say activists want to avenge IRA attacks.
On the other side of the border, Irish police said they had uncovered an IRA training camp including an underground firing range in the village of Scotstown in County Monaghan.
The camp was found in a three-week-old search of the border area for arms dumps used by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) in its 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland.
Irish republicans marked the anniversary of the Easter uprising in Dublin which led to the end of British rule with parades and rallies across the island of Ireland.
Northern Ireland's police chief, Ronnie Flanagan, said that resurgent IRA violence had created "a very dangerous situation" in the province.

Chief Constable Flanagan dismissed media suggestions that the Irish Republican Army was engaged in shadow boxing in the runup to British elections on May 1 and said the guerrillas were mounting "real attacks with a determination to kill."

Flanagan was speaking to Sky television the day after security forces found a 1,000-lb (500 kg) bomb abandoned in a country road where it was being assembled to ambush British soldiers from the nearby Ballykinler army base.

Superintendent Sam Martin said nine plastic bags of fertiliser-based explosive and detonators were being put together in an attempt to cause "appalling injury or death to passers-by." No-one claimed responsibility for the device but it was thought to be the latest attempted attack on British targets of the IRA in defiance of appeals by Britain, Ireland and the United States to declare a new ceasefire.

Labour's spokeswoman on Northern Ireland, Mo Mowlam, told the British Broadcasting Corporation that a truce called now would allow sufficient time to elapse for the authorities to determine it was genuine and allow Sinn Fein to the talks.
Her words appeared to signal no change in the policy adopted by Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government but a Sinn Fein spokesman said Mowlam's comments were "encouraging."
